metadata.title: Claude, Matter Intake.
metadata.subtitle: What a Skill Actually Is
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: does Claude gain judgment about which matters to take on when it picks up the matter-intake skill? Lands the carry-out that a skill is a fixed set of questions Claude asks and logs the same way every time, not a decision.

beats.narration_text: A newcomer to a legal practice hears 'Claude has a matter-intake skill' and reads it as screening — Claude deciding which matters are worth taking. That misreads the machinery. The actual job is narrower: log the answers to a fixed set of questions, the same way, every time. Liam, in for Bear — let's take it apart.

beats.narration_text: Here's the natural first read of the name. Claude has a matter-intake skill — so Claude must be screening new matters, deciding which ones are worth the firm's risk before anyone else looks. The word 'intake' implies a gate. The word 'skill' implies judgment. Put them together and you get 'AI that picks the cases.'

Now watch it break. Feed matter-intake a matter with an obvious conflict of interest and the skill doesn't refuse it, doesn't flag it declined, doesn't even hesitate. It asks the same nine questions and writes down the answers exactly the way it would on any other matter. The decision to decline was always the lawyer's — the skill was never wired to make it. What looked like a gate is a form.

production_viz.label: STILL JUST LOGS IT
production_viz.caption: the decline call is the lawyer's

beats.narration_text: Here's what matter-intake actually does, mechanism side. One uniform set of questions — nine of them, in this order: identification, conflicts, source, risk, materiality, outside counsel, owners, legal hold, key dates. The same nine, every matter. Watch this list — it comes back at the end. They optimized for uniformity at the expense of cleverness: no branching, no skipping, no matter-type-specific detours.

The runtime is boring on purpose. Claude reads the SKILL.md, then works the nine questions top to bottom — no branching, no conditional logic — and turns the answers into two files: matter.md, which reads like a human summary, and history.md, which is the interview transcript. Then one structured row gets appended to a running log, _log.yaml — a machine-readable index across every matter that ever passed through. Same three artifacts, same order, every time.

production_viz.label: READ, THEN LOG IN ORDER
production_viz.caption: top to bottom, then written down

beats.narration_text: That's what makes matter-intake a specification, not a judgment call. The payoff of the design: identical intake, every matter, every lawyer — the record is uniform because the questions are. The cost: the skill only structures what's told to it. Nothing in the file decides whether the matter gets taken on; that call stays outside the file, with the human. This works if you value auditability; it fails if you wanted the AI to do the picking.

So the anchor returns. Matter-intake never screens a matter for you. What it guarantees is smaller and more useful: whichever lawyer runs it, the same nine questions get asked in the same order and the same two files plus one log row get written. Identification, conflicts, source, risk, materiality, outside counsel, owners, legal hold, key dates. That's the whole trick — a shape enforced on the record, not a decision automated out of your hands.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — SAME NINE, EVERY RUN

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — SAME NINE, EVERY RUN
production_viz.caption: same nine questions, every run

beats.narration_text: The design is honest about its own limits in both directions. Watching matter-intake come back clean on every field doesn't prove the matter is actually conflict-free — it only proves the checklist was filled in. And a flagged risk field doesn't prove there's a real problem — it may just be a case the lawyer still has to judge. Read it as evidence that the interview happened, not as a verdict on what was said.
A skill named matter-intake doesn't decide which matters to take — it's a fixed set of questions Claude asks and logs the same way every time, so the accept-or-decline call is still yours.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's a prompt — paste it into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. I want to understand what a Claude skill actually is versus what its name suggests. Pick one recurring decision I make the same way every time before it starts — say, whether to open a new client file, or approve a routine internal request. Do three things: draft the SKILL dot MD for it in plain language, with the fixed questions in the exact order they should be asked; name the two files the skill should write and the one row it should append to a running log; and mark which parts of the decision the skill cannot make for me, so the accept-or-decline call stays where it belongs. Go deeper: look at a workflow you already trust to a checklist — is the checklist enforcing shape, or quietly making the decision, and which of those did you actually want?
